extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and readers interested in moral fiction and literary ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the principles John Gardner sets out about what constitutes 'moral fiction' — how fiction should test values, serve ethics, and relate to art and criticism. The page is a catalog/record for the book that indicates the book's principal thematic chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: great moral fiction has open-mindedly tested human values
rubrics_metrics.description: Great moral fiction has open-mindedly tested human values in an attempt to discover what best promotes human fulfillment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page summary: the central standard is that moral fiction should actively and openly test values with the aim of discovering what promotes human fulfillment. Full development, examples, and argumentation for this standard appear in the book itself (access-restricted on this catalog page).

rubrics_metrics.name: current fiction fails to test values and thus undermines literature and faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Current fiction fails to test human values and, thus, undermines our experience of literature and our faith in ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented on the page as the book's thesis/diagnosis — a negative criterion/anti-pattern: work that avoids genuinely testing values or that diminishes moral inquiry is judged harmful to literary experience. The book presumably elaborates on why and how this is so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premises on Art and Morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter/topic heading indicating a set of foundational claims about the relationship between art and morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table of contents lists this chapter; it implies the book articulates premises to use when evaluating whether fiction is moral. The catalog entry does not include the chapter text; consult the book for explicit premises and criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Art and Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter/topic heading indicating principles governing art and the practice of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests Gardner provides standards/principles critics and writers should use when judging or producing art. The catalog page only lists the chapter title; details are in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter/topic heading focused on defining and exemplifying 'moral fiction' as a category or ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a TOC entry, this denotes extended treatment of what counts as moral fiction, likely offering criteria, examples, and distinctions. Full criteria are inside the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter/topic heading concerning the practice of criticism that addresses moral aspects of literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies guidance for critics on how to evaluate literature's moral dimensions. The catalog record does not provide the chapter content.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Artist as Critic and Art and Insanity
rubrics_metrics.description: TOC headings indicating discussion of the artist's role in criticism and the relation between art and mental illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These headings signal that Gardner treats the responsibilities/stance of the artist-as-critic and examines how art intersects with insanity; they imply evaluative standards (e.g., what an artist-critic should do, how to judge portrayals of madness). The page lists these topics but does not supply the substantive guidance.
